paragraphs: Deep networks succeed partly by changing how inputs are represented across layers. Yet standard infinite-width theories remove this learning of representations, making them a poor fit for explaining that part of deep learning. This paper develops a different infinite-width limit that retains representation learning resembling finite-width models while preserving some mathematical simplicity.

For deep Gaussian processes, the new limit produces exactly multivariate Gaussian posterior distributions. Their covariances come from optimizing an interpretable objective: a likelihood term rewards predictive performance, while a sequence of divergence terms discourages departures from the prior. Experiments with wide but finite deep Gaussian processes support these theoretical results.

The authors also turn this framework into deep kernel machines, a flexible extension of kernel methods with multiple learned representation stages. The straightforward version has computational cost growing cubically with dataset size. A sparse version uses inducing-point techniques to make that dependence linear. Extensions to neural networks are also presented, although their posterior distributions are not Gaussian.
icml-2023-a-theory-of-representation-lea.tldr: A new infinite-width theory preserves representation learning and leads to deep kernel machines with a scalable sparse variant.

paragraphs: Neural collapse describes a pattern in well-trained networks: examples carrying the same label end up with almost identical final-layer representations. Taken literally, this suggests that labels determine those representations and that finer structure in the inputs disappears. This paper investigates the small differences that remain beneath that apparent collapse.

The authors train a network on CIFAR-10 after merging its ten classes into five broader labels. Once training converges, they use unsupervised clustering of the learned representations to recover the original ten classes. The reconstructed labels reach 93% test accuracy, nearly matching ordinary ten-class training with the same architecture. Thus, variation that looks small can still carry substantial information about distinctions absent from the training labels.

An initial theoretical result also demonstrates fine-grained representation structure in a simplified synthetic setting. Together, these findings show why apparent collapse is an incomplete account of what a network retains: input structure can remain influential within the tight clusters associated with labels.
icml-2023-are-neurons-actually-collapsed.tldr: Small variations beneath apparent neural collapse can retain enough input structure to recover classes never supplied as training labels.

paragraphs: An agent trained only on recorded experience can misjudge actions that fall outside that experience. Online fine-tuning can correct these estimates, but obtaining new interactions may be inaccessible or dangerous in settings such as healthcare and autonomous driving. This paper proposes Offline-with-Action-Preferences, or OAP, to improve offline training without additional environment interactions.

OAP queries preferences between actions in the collected data and actions proposed by the learned policy. It uses those preferences to strengthen or relax the constraint that keeps the policy close to recorded behavior. This helps distinguish an action whose apparent value is overestimated from one that represents a useful improvement, supporting more accurate evaluation of unseen data.

The authors prove a lower bound on the improvement over the behavior policy and evaluate OAP with leading algorithms on D4RL. They report scores averaging 29% higher, with a 98% increase on challenging AntMaze tasks. These results support action preferences as a potentially valuable alternative to online correction in the evaluated settings.
icml-2023-boosting-offline-reinforcement.tldr: OAP uses action-preference queries to improve offline reinforcement learning without collecting new environment interactions.

paragraphs: Models often struggle on subgroups that received little representation during training. However, changes in subgroup composition can arise through different mechanisms, and a method that handles one mechanism may struggle with another. This paper develops a unified framework for distinguishing these shifts and examining how robustness methods behave across them.

The benchmark evaluates 20 algorithms on 12 real-world datasets spanning vision, language, and healthcare, using results from more than 10,000 trained models. It finds that existing algorithms improve subgroup robustness for some shift types but not others. That finding makes the kind of shift an important part of interpreting a method’s reported success.

The study also finds that selecting models by their weakest class accuracy can work surprisingly well without subgroup annotations. Finally, it demonstrates a tradeoff between worst-group accuracy and other important metrics. Improving the weakest subgroup therefore does not settle every evaluation question; the chosen metrics determine which aspects of performance are rewarded and which tradeoffs remain visible.
icml-2023-change-is-hard-a-closer-look-a.tldr: A large benchmark shows that subgroup robustness depends on the shift mechanism, model-selection rule, and evaluation metrics.

paragraphs: A language model can perform an unfamiliar task by reading input-output demonstrations in its prompt, without changing its parameters. Which demonstrations it sees strongly affects performance. This paper studies how to choose those examples systematically, treating the prompt’s demonstration set as something to optimize rather than assemble through simple heuristics.

The proposed method, CEIL, formulates example selection as a subset-selection problem. It uses determinantal point processes to model interactions involving the current input and candidate demonstrations. A contrastive learning procedure draws preference information from language models to train the selection process. The central idea is to account for how examples work together within a set.

The authors evaluate CEIL on 12 datasets covering seven language tasks, including classification, question answering, code generation, and semantic parsing. They report evidence of effectiveness, transferability, and compositionality. These findings support learning a demonstration-selection strategy that captures relationships among examples, making the composition of the prompt an explicit part of improving in-context learning.
icml-2023-compositional-exemplars-for-in.tldr: CEIL learns to select demonstration sets for language-model prompts by modeling how examples work together.

paragraphs: An agent learning tasks sequentially needs both plasticity, to adapt to new tasks, and stability, to retain earlier knowledge. CoTASP addresses this tension by assigning tasks to selected parts of a shared policy network. It learns dictionaries that produce sparse masks, with each mask acting as a prompt that selects a task’s subnetwork.

Training alternates between adjusting the prompts and adjusting the selected network weights. The dictionary is then updated to connect optimized prompts with task embeddings, capturing semantic relationships among tasks. Related tasks consequently share more neurons through similar prompts, while the allocation mechanism restrains interference that could cause forgetting.

For a new task, the trained dictionaries and shared policy support adaptation through sparse prompting and subnetwork fine-tuning. Experiments report a favorable balance between adaptation and retention without storing or replaying earlier experience. In the evaluated comparisons, CoTASP outperforms existing continual and multitask reinforcement-learning methods on seen-task performance, forgetting reduction, and generalization to unseen tasks.
icml-2023-continual-task-allocation-in-m.tldr: CoTASP assigns related tasks overlapping subnetworks through sparse prompts to support adaptation while reducing forgetting.

paragraphs: Adversarial corruption makes learning from feedback harder because some observations can deliberately mislead the learner. Existing guarantees discussed here either restrict the model to linear functions or let the corruption penalty grow with the square root of the number of rounds. This paper develops methods for more general function approximation with a better dependence on corruption.

For contextual bandits, the proposed computationally efficient algorithm combines uncertainty-weighted least-squares regression with a new uncertainty estimator for general function classes. Its regret scales like the square root of the number of rounds plus the total corruption, up to logarithmic factors. The corruption contribution is additive, rather than multiplied by the time-dependent term.

A new analysis controls accumulated weighted uncertainty without relying on linear structure. The authors extend the approach to episodic Markov decision processes, again obtaining additive corruption dependence. Across settings where the corruption amount is known or unknown, the reported guarantees either nearly match lower bounds or improve existing bounds across corruption levels.
icml-2023-corruption-robust-algorithms-w.tldr: Uncertainty weighting yields nonlinear bandit and reinforcement-learning guarantees with an additive penalty for adversarial corruption.

paragraphs: Graph matching asks which vertex in one graph corresponds to which vertex in another. This paper studies two correlated stochastic block models, where vertices have community structure. Such matching matters in applications including social-network de-anonymization, but community structure complicates the task relative to simpler random-graph models with existing efficient matching guarantees.

The proposed algorithm compares partition trees rooted at individual vertices. Each tree divides a vertex’s large neighborhood into disjoint groups using statistics about connections to different communities. These partitions provide structured information for comparing candidate counterparts across the two graphs. The method extends an earlier partition-tree approach to account for communities.

The authors prove that their algorithm achieves exact matching with high probability for dense correlated stochastic block models with constant edge correlation. They identify it as the first low-order polynomial-time algorithm with that guarantee in this setting. The result combines computational efficiency with recovery of the full correspondence, under the stated random-graph and density conditions.
icml-2023-efficient-algorithms-for-exact.tldr: Community-aware partition trees enable efficient exact matching of dense correlated stochastic block models with high probability.

paragraphs: Federated learning combines contributions from clients whose datasets may contain very different proportions of categories. Common aggregation rules give clients influence according to dataset size. This paper argues, through empirical observations and theoretical analysis, that size alone is not optimal when local category distributions differ from the global distribution.

FedDisco adjusts aggregation weights using both dataset size and a measure of the discrepancy between local and global category distributions. These two signals provide complementary information: the quantity of local data and how its category mix differs from the overall mix. The resulting weights also contribute to a tighter theoretical upper bound on optimization error.

Experiments show FedDisco outperforming several leading methods and improving performance when incorporated into existing approaches. The authors describe the method as efficient in communication and computation, with a modular design. Its contribution is to make the aggregation rule itself responsive to category imbalance, providing another way to address heterogeneity alongside changes to local training or global fine-tuning.
icml-2023-feddisco-federated-learning-wi.tldr: FedDisco improves federated aggregation by weighting clients using both dataset size and category-distribution discrepancy.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to infer causal relationships from observational time series when some confounding variables are hidden. It assumes a stationary structural vector autoregressive process in discrete time. The causal structure can include both relationships across time steps and contemporaneous relationships between variables within the same time step.

The proposed constraint-based algorithm gradually refines a causal graph in a particular order. It learns longer-term temporal relationships first, moves toward shorter-term relationships, and considers contemporaneous relationships last. This ordering reduces the number of statistical tests required. The key methodological choice is therefore how to organize the discovery process across different temporal distances.

Experiments confirm the reduction in testing and associate it with higher causal-discovery accuracy on synthetic data. For real-world data, the resulting graphs are reported to be more plausible than those from leading alternatives. These findings support ordered refinement as a useful approach within the assumed time-series setting, while the real-data claim concerns plausibility rather than verified recovery of every causal relationship.
icml-2023-from-temporal-to-contemporaneo.tldr: Learning long-term causal links before shorter-term and simultaneous links reduces testing and improves time-series causal discovery.

paragraphs: Equivariant neural networks build symmetry into their predictions, but using them normally requires deciding in advance which symmetry applies. That choice can be difficult in scientific applications, and enforcing an inappropriate symmetry can hurt performance. LieGAN addresses this problem by learning candidate symmetries directly from a dataset.

Its training resembles a generative adversarial setup. A generator learns a group of transformations and applies them to the data, while a discriminator tries to distinguish the transformed distribution from the original. The generator seeks transformations that preserve the distribution and fool the discriminator. Learned symmetries are expressed as an interpretable Lie algebra basis, making the discovered transformation structure explicit.

The paper demonstrates discovery of symmetries including rotation groups and the restricted Lorentz group in trajectory prediction and top-quark tagging tasks. It also shows that learned symmetries can be incorporated into several existing equivariant networks to improve prediction accuracy and generalization. This connects symmetry discovery to models that can use the discovered structure.
icml-2023-generative-adversarial-symmetr.tldr: LieGAN learns interpretable symmetry groups from data through adversarial training and uses them to improve equivariant prediction models.

paragraphs: Large integer programs can strain optimization methods that repeatedly rely on a large solver. This paper examines a framework combining graph neural networks with large neighborhood search and identifies two bottlenecks: incomplete use of learned embedding information and continued dependence on solving large optimization subproblems. It proposes a three-stage alternative.

First, a multitask graph neural network builds an embedding space. Next, a gradient-boosted decision-tree model uses information in that space to make predictions. Finally, neighborhood optimization uses a smaller optimizer to tackle the larger problem. The design connects learned representations and predictions to the optimization stage, aiming to make a limited-size solver useful at much larger scales.

Experiments report solving million-scale integer programs and outperforming SCIP and Gurobi within the specified wall-clock budget using an optimizer handling 30% of the problem size. The framework also achieves the same solution quality as SCIP with 99% less running time in reported comparisons. These results concern solution quality under the evaluated computational budgets.
icml-2023-gnn-gbdt-guided-fast-optimizin.tldr: A three-stage learning-guided framework uses a smaller optimizer to solve large integer programs efficiently in reported experiments.

paragraphs: A recommendation platform’s behavior can change as creators compete and adapt their content strategies. This paper asks how much that competition can reduce user welfare when the platform recommends its top K items according to relevance. It studies the long-term interaction between the recommendation policy, user choices, and creator learning.

The model assumes that user decisions follow a Random Utility model and that creators update their strategies using arbitrary no-regret learning algorithms, without requiring explicit creator utility functions. The analysis uses Price of Anarchy to quantify welfare loss caused by competition. It proves that the lost fraction is bounded by a small constant depending on K and the randomness in user decisions.

The authors also prove that this bound is tight. The result identifies a benefit of relevance-driven recommendations under the modeled conditions: competition need not destroy most user welfare when decisions contain randomness and the platform offers reasonably many alternatives. Those conditions are central to interpreting the guarantee and its dependence on recommendation breadth.
icml-2023-how-bad-is-top-k-recommendatio.tldr: Under a specified creator-learning and user-choice model, top-K recommendations have a tight bound on welfare loss from competition.

paragraphs: Hyperbolic representation learning often assumes that optimization will automatically discover and preserve the hierarchy underlying the data. This paper questions that assumption and introduces a mechanism for tracking where representations move in hyperbolic space. Applying it to existing models reveals learned representations that the authors find suboptimal.

The proposed remedy, hyperbolic informed embedding or HIE, uses hierarchical information inferred from each node’s hyperbolic distance to the origin. This distance, also called the induced hyperbolic norm, provides a signal already available from the representation. HIE incorporates that signal into existing models to guide their embeddings more explicitly, rather than relying entirely on the ordinary optimization process to capture hierarchy.

The method is designed to work across tasks and model architectures. Experiments spanning different models and tasks support this flexibility and report improvements of up to 21.4% over competing baselines. The maximum reported gain illustrates the method’s potential, while the broader finding is that explicitly using the available geometric hierarchy signal can improve existing hyperbolic representations.
icml-2023-hyperbolic-representation-lear.tldr: HIE improves hyperbolic embeddings by explicitly using hierarchical information inferred from distance to the origin.

paragraphs: Physics-informed neural networks solve partial differential equations by minimizing losses for both the equation and its boundary conditions. Training can become difficult when these losses have imbalanced scales, and understanding what a low training loss implies about actual solution error requires theory. This paper addresses both the analysis and the optimization problem.

The authors analyze second-order non-homogeneous equations, organizing them into three categories that cover various common problems. They connect training loss with actual error and establish convergence under mild conditions. This analysis motivates MultiAdam, a scale-invariant optimizer that uses gradient momentum to balance the different loss terms separately for each network parameter.

Balancing at the parameter level makes the optimizer’s treatment of competing losses more fine-grained than a single overall weighting choice. Experiments across several physical domains report predictive-accuracy improvements of one to two orders of magnitude over strong baselines. The results support the proposed optimizer on the tested problems, while the convergence claim remains tied to the conditions of the theoretical analysis.
icml-2023-multiadam-parameter-wise-scale.tldr: MultiAdam balances physics-informed training losses for each parameter, with theory linking loss to solution error and substantial reported accuracy gains.

paragraphs: Raven’s Progressive Matrices test visual reasoning through patterns that require an appropriate missing answer. This paper proposes a neural architecture inspired by prediction error in neuroscience. The model reasons by predicting what an answer’s features should look like and comparing that prediction with the features of candidate answers.

A reasoning block uses convolution to extract abstract rules from high-level features of eight context images. It generates predicted answer features, computes their differences from the eight candidates, and passes those prediction errors to the next stage. Integrating these blocks into a residual network produces the Predictive Reasoning Network, or PredRNet.

Experiments report leading average performance on several major matrix-reasoning benchmarks, along with good generalization in varied out-of-distribution settings and other visual reasoning tasks. The model also develops low-dimensional representations of abstract rules and reduces hierarchical prediction errors during training. These observations support prediction-error minimization as a useful mechanism for artificial visual reasoning and illustrate the potential of neuroscience-inspired architecture design.
icml-2023-neural-prediction-errors-enabl.tldr: PredRNet uses hierarchical differences between predicted and candidate answer features to solve abstract visual reasoning problems.

paragraphs: This paper asks what pre-training across reinforcement-learning environments can contribute when an agent must perform in a target environment. Its analysis distinguishes reinforcement-learning generalization from supervised generalization and establishes the need for target-environment fine-tuning for good test performance in the studied setting. The question then becomes how much pre-training can improve that adaptation.

The authors establish an asymptotic limitation: as the relevant learning regime becomes asymptotic, pre-training can improve performance by at most a constant factor. This places a ceiling on the long-run benefit captured by their analysis. It does not erase the possibility of useful gains when the learner has a finite amount of experience.

For that finite-experience regime, the paper introduces a policy collection-elimination algorithm and proves a distribution-dependent regret bound independent of the state-action space. This provides a constructive result showing how pre-training can help efficient fine-tuning. Together, the two results distinguish a limit on asymptotic improvement from provable benefits in the non-asymptotic regime.
icml-2023-on-the-power-of-pre-training-f.tldr: The theory limits pre-training’s asymptotic benefit in reinforcement learning while proving useful gains for finite-experience fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Personalized federated learning aims to give each client a useful individual model while benefiting from collaboration. Deciding who should collaborate matters when clients have different data or when some clients are malicious. This paper proposes learning a collaboration graph that represents the benefit and strength of each pairwise relationship.

The resulting algorithm, pFedGraph, divides the work between server and clients. The server infers the graph using pairwise model similarity and dataset size. Each client then optimizes its local model with help from an aggregated model. The graph steers clients toward stronger collaboration with similar, beneficial partners while the local optimization supports personalization.

Experiments compare pFedGraph with 14 baseline methods across different levels of data heterogeneity and multiple settings containing malicious clients. The authors report consistent improvements in these evaluations. The approach makes collaboration itself adaptive, helping explain its reported ability to handle both variation among clients and model-poisoning attacks without treating every potential partner as equally useful.
icml-2023-personalized-federated-learnin.tldr: pFedGraph learns which clients should collaborate and how strongly to improve personalized federated learning under heterogeneous and malicious-client settings.

paragraphs: Mean-field games approximate interactions among many symmetric, anonymous players. However, existing learning guarantees often assume access to a mechanism that can arbitrarily modify the population distribution. This paper develops guarantees using observations from the actual N-player simulator, avoiding that population-level control and allowing agents to learn independently.

The method uses policy mirror ascent. The analysis constructs a contractive operator whose fixed point is the Nash equilibrium, using the mirror-ascent map rather than a best-response map. It also analyzes temporal-difference learning along a single sample path. These ingredients connect equilibrium computation with learning from one trajectory of the interacting agents.

For the regularized game, the authors establish convergence with sample requirements scaling approximately as the inverse square of the target error, up to logarithmic factors. A standard mean-field approximation error of order one over the square root of N remains. The contribution is a finite-sample guarantee for independent learning that does not require arbitrary manipulation of the population distribution.
icml-2023-policy-mirror-ascent-for-effic.tldr: Policy mirror ascent enables independently learning agents to approach a regularized mean-field equilibrium from a single trajectory with finite-sample guarantees.

paragraphs: Multimodal generators that store all their knowledge in model parameters need increasing model capacity and training data to capture more information. This paper proposes giving a generator access to relevant images and text retrieved from an external memory. The aim is to make access to knowledge more modular and scalable.

The resulting model, RA-CM3, uses a pretrained CLIP retriever and a CM3 Transformer generator trained on LAION. Retrieved material provides context for generation, and the system can both retrieve and produce text and images. This makes external multimodal information part of the generation process, alongside the knowledge encoded during training.

On MS-COCO, the authors report improvements of 12 FID and 17 CIDEr over baseline multimodal models, covering image and caption generation. Training uses less than 30% of DALL-E’s compute in the reported comparison. The model also demonstrates faithful image generation and multimodal in-context learning, including generating images from demonstrations. These findings support retrieval as a useful component of multimodal generation.
icml-2023-retrieval-augmented-multimodal.tldr: RA-CM3 retrieves relevant text and images to improve multimodal generation while using substantially less training compute in reported comparisons.

paragraphs: Early event prediction aims to warn about an event before it occurs while keeping false alarms low. Treating each observation as an isolated binary classification example ignores relationships across time. This paper uses that temporal structure to improve prediction, motivated by the requirements of medical decision-support systems.

The authors first introduce a theoretical framework connecting dynamic survival analysis with early event prediction. Comparing objectives from these areas leads to Temporal Label Smoothing, or TLS. The method preserves prediction monotonicity over time and concentrates the training objective on regions with a stronger predictive signal. Its design makes the temporal organization of the task part of how the model learns.

On two large benchmark tasks, TLS outperforms all evaluated baselines. Gains are especially notable for clinically relevant measures such as event recall when false-alarm rates are low. The reported reduction in missed events reaches a factor of two relative to previously used approaches. This connects the training change to the practical goal of catching more events without excessive alarms.
icml-2023-temporal-label-smoothing-for-e.tldr: Temporal Label Smoothing uses time structure to improve early event detection, with fewer missed events at low false-alarm rates.

paragraphs: Active learning seeks the most valuable examples to label so that a model can learn effectively from fewer annotations. Data augmentation can broaden exploration of the input space and help identify useful examples. This paper studies how to combine the two through a controlled framework called CAMPAL.

CAMPAL separates augmentation policies for the labeled and unlabeled data pools, making their treatment purposeful rather than uniform. It also provides controlled augmentation strengths that can be quantitatively optimized. The framework is designed to accommodate a broad range of active-learning schemes, and theoretical developments inform its key components. Together, these choices make augmentation an adjustable part of the selection process.

Extensive experiments report improved performance for active-learning methods, including an absolute boost of 16.99% on CIFAR-10 with 1,000 annotated samples and additional gains on SVHN. The findings support careful coordination between augmentation and active learning: choosing where and how strongly to augment can improve the value extracted from a limited annotation budget.
icml-2023-towards-controlled-data-augmen.tldr: CAMPAL improves active learning through separate augmentation policies and optimizable augmentation strengths for labeled and unlabeled data.

paragraphs: Quantum approaches offer a possible route to solving difficult combinatorial optimization problems. However, the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm was originally designed for unconstrained problems and jointly searches for circuit parameters and solutions through time-consuming iterations. This paper explores supervised quantum learning as an alternative for problems with explicit constraints.

The proposed QAP-QNN targets the quadratic assignment problem, accounting for matching constraints and the requirement that relabeling graph nodes should not change the underlying problem. It translates the optimization problem into constrained vertex classification. This reformulation lets a quantum neural network learn the task in a supervised manner while incorporating the structure that valid assignments must respect.

The authors evaluate graph matching and the Traveling Salesman Problem using TorchQuantum simulators and report empirical evidence of effectiveness. The contribution is a quantum-learning formulation for constrained optimization and a demonstration on two tasks. The evidence is simulation-based; the abstract presents quantum advantage as a potential motivation rather than an achieved experimental result.
icml-2023-towards-quantum-machine-learni.tldr: QAP-QNN reframes constrained quadratic assignment as supervised quantum vertex classification and demonstrates effectiveness in simulation.

paragraphs: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning trains an agent to pursue different goals using a fixed dataset. Remaining conservative around recorded experience is one challenge; achieving goals outside the training distribution is another. This paper investigates that second challenge through both experiments and theory, asking which design choices support generalization to unseen goals.

Across a number of experiments, weighted imitation learning generalizes better than a pessimism-based offline reinforcement-learning method. The authors use this observation to develop a theory of out-of-distribution generalization that characterizes several important design choices. They then combine the theoretical and empirical findings into GOAT, a new offline goal-conditioned learning method.

Evaluation uses a new benchmark with nine tasks drawn from the training distribution and 17 out-of-distribution tasks. GOAT outperforms current leading methods by a large margin on that benchmark. The results support the paper’s combined design approach and show why unseen-goal performance deserves explicit attention when developing agents from offline data, beyond the concern of staying close to recorded behavior.
icml-2023-what-is-essential-for-unseen-g.tldr: GOAT combines theoretical and empirical insights about offline goal generalization to improve performance on unseen-goal benchmarks.

paragraphs: When training labels contain errors, one approach keeps confident examples labeled and treats uncertain examples as unlabeled data for semi-supervised learning. Another explicitly models label noise to construct statistically consistent classifiers. This paper asks how to choose between these approaches for a particular application by examining the process that generated the data.

Its analysis identifies causal direction as important for the semi-supervised approach. Performance depends heavily on the data-generating process, whereas the label-noise-modeling approach is not affected by that process in the paper’s analysis. In particular, when the features causally determine the label, the authors state that the semi-supervised approach would not help.

The paper also provides an intuitive method for discovering the causal structure when it is unknown and the dataset contains noisy labels. This turns the comparison into a question about the dataset’s generation mechanism, rather than relying only on which method appears attractive in isolation. The contribution is guidance for matching a noisy-label learning strategy to the causal structure of the application.
icml-2023-which-is-better-for-learning-w.tldr: The paper uses causal data-generation structure to explain when semi-supervised learning helps with noisy labels and when explicit noise modeling is preferable.
